verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents, of David. I rejoiced in those saying to me: The house of YHWH, let us go.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing road, David's. Gladness came over me, and it came at a sound: voices, close at hand, saying to me, "To the house of the LORD, let us go!"
verses.directors_commentary:
The line is a spoken memory, not a report: the singer replays the moment when the invitation reached him, and the whole psalm grows from that one sentence. Play it as a person remembering the exact words, a little breathless. The pilgrim feasts of the old Israelite year (Passover, Weeks, Booths) drew families up to Jerusalem, so "let us go" is a village or a household turning together onto the road, and the speaker hears it as joy rather than duty.

The KJV's "I was glad when they said" is a neat past tense, but the Hebrew says "I rejoiced in those saying", a participle: the joy sits in the voices, and the invitation is still sounding. The KJV also adds "into"; the Hebrew has no preposition at all, only the bare "house of YHWH, let us go", as if the destination itself is the verb's object. Note also that the title "Song of the Ascents" (the KJV's "Song of degrees" is the old word for steps) names the pilgrim's climb up to Jerusalem; the Hebrew מַעֲלוֹת is built on the root "go up" that returns in verse 4.

philological_notes.note: 'The ascents', from the root 'to go up'. The label is shared by Psalms 120-134. Whether it means the steps of the Temple, the pilgrims' climb or a rising musical pattern is not settled; the root links it to עָלוּ in verse 4. The Targum in the packet reads it differently, as 'ascents of the abyss'.
A participle 'in those saying', with bet of cause after 'rejoice'. The joy is located in the speakers' act of speaking, which the KJV's past 'when they said' loses.

verses.translation_literal: Standing they were, our feet, in your gates, Jerusalem.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now our feet are standing, standing still, here in your gates, Jerusalem.
verses.directors_commentary:
The pilgrims have arrived, and the first thing the verse gives us is their feet. Hebrew puts the participle "standing" first and the feet after it, so the stillness comes before the body: they stop dead on the threshold. A city gate in the ancient Near East was a deep, roofed passage with benches, the place of trade, of the elders' judgment, of news; to stand in the gates is to be inside the city's public life, and for a country pilgrim it is the first touch of the place.

The KJV's "shall stand" turns a completed arrival into a future promise, and ASV's "are standing" changes the Hebrew perfect "were standing" into a present. The Hebrew reads "they were standing", a state looked back on, which keeps the psalm in the voice of memory begun in verse 1. Jerusalem is addressed directly ("your gates"), the first of several turns to the city as "you"; have the actors speak to it as to a person.

philological_notes.note: A participle with the perfect of 'to be': 'they were standing'. It describes a state reached and remembered, not a future vow as in the KJV 'shall stand'. Meiri also hears 'standing' as 'enduring', and Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David as pausing in the crowd at the gates.

verses.translation_literal: Jerusalem, the built-up one, like a city that was joined to itself together.
verses.translation_dramatic: Jerusalem, built up, built close: a city knitted to itself, every house leaning on the next.
verses.directors_commentary:
The singer now stands in the gate and looks at the city, and the tone shifts from arrival to wonder. The key word is the verb "joined" (חֻבְּרָה): a city that is bound to itself, with no gap in it. Most ancient cities of the hill country were loose clusters of walled villages; a dense, joined city was a marvel, and the pilgrim's eye reads the tight rows of houses as unity. The ancient interpreters in the packet hear two further things in it: that the tribes are gathered into one body in this city (Ibn Ezra, Malbim), and that the earthly city answers to a heavenly one (Rashi citing Taanit 5a; the Targum says so outright).

The KJV's "is builded as a city that is compact together" is serviceable, but "compact" is an archaism for "joined", and the Hebrew piles up the idea of union: "joined", "to itself", "together" (יַחְדָּו), three words for one closeness. The Hebrew also says "the built one", a title: Jerusalem is the one that is built, as if building were its name.

philological_notes.note: A relative with the late prefix she- ('that'), then a passive verb: 'that was joined'. The root means to join or ally; the same root underlies 'companion' (חָבֵר). The sense here is a city whose parts are fastened together. The prefix she- instead of 'asher is common in the later psalms.

The article plus a passive participle: 'the built-up one', a title for the city. Meiri gives several readings, including 'built from sons', playing on בנה and בן, which is a rabbinic wordplay and not the plain sense.

verses.translation_literal: Where there went up tribes, tribes of Yah, a testimony to Israel, to give thanks to the name of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: For this is where they climbed, tribe after tribe, the tribes of Yah, as a witness to Israel, to give thanks, and the thanks go to the Name of the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse explains why the city matters: it is where the tribes go up. The Hebrew repeats "tribes" (שבטים ... שבטי), so the word lands twice, once bare and once with the divine name attached. Say it like a roll call; the twelve tribes of Israel were a confederation of kin groups, and the three yearly pilgrimages were the one occasion on which they stood in the same courtyard. "Yah" is the short form of YHWH, used here in a compressed, almost chanted phrase; keep it as a different sound from the full Name later in the verse.

The KJV "unto the testimony of Israel" reads עֵדוּת as a thing Israel owns; the Hebrew says "a testimony to (or for) Israel", and the clause has no verb, so it could equally be "an ordinance for Israel", as ASV prefers. The Hebrew word עֵדוּת is the same as the "testimony" of the ark, the tablets of the covenant, so both readings carry weight. The KJV also reads "go up" in the present; the Hebrew perfect looks back to the habit of the festivals. And note that Hebrew says to give thanks to "the name" of YHWH, not to YHWH directly, a mark of the Temple's theology of the divine Name dwelling in the house.

philological_notes.note: 'Testimony', 'witness', also the 'decree' or 'ordinance'. The ark is called 'the ark of the testimony' (Exod 25:22). Here it floats without a verb, so the line can be read as 'it is a testimony to Israel' or 'an ordinance for Israel'. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as divine witness to Israel; Radak and Ibn Ezra as a command to appear.
An infinitive of the root that means both 'to give thanks' and 'to confess, acknowledge'; the Hebrew has one word for both. The KJV 'give thanks' catches half of it.

verses.translation_literal: For there sat thrones for judgment, thrones for the house of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For here the thrones sit, the thrones of judgment, thrones of the house of David, in the very city they have climbed to.
verses.directors_commentary:
Say 'thrones' twice and let the repetition land: the verse is a pair of beats, judgment first, David second. The psalmists' Jerusalem is not only a shrine but a court. In the ancient Near East a king's throne was the place where the weak could be heard against the strong, and in Israel's law the hardest cases went up to the place the LORD chose (Deut 17:8-9); Jehoshaphat later set judges in Jerusalem for exactly this (2 Chr 19:8-11). Pilgrims arriving here are arriving at the end of the road for justice, and the line should carry that relief.

The KJV's 'are set thrones of judgment' turns the Hebrew into a passive scene, furniture arranged. The Hebrew is active: thrones 'sat', as if the seats themselves were seated and presiding. 'There' (shamah) also carries a faint sense of direction, 'to there', the place the tribes climbed towards in verse 4. Radak hears a double meaning in the plural, one throne for the Shekhinah and one for the dynasty; Rashi, quoting the Tanhuma, takes the first thrones as judging the nations. Play it as plain, grave pride: justice and David sit in the same city.

philological_notes.note: 'Thrones', repeated in the second half of the verse, so that the line is built on the repeated word. The subject of 'sat' is the thrones themselves, so the verb is active ('thrones sat'), not the passive 'are set' of the KJV. Radak finds in the plural one throne for the Shekhinah and one for the kingship of David's house.

'For judgment': the thrones exist to give justice, and the word covers both the verdict and the court's whole function. Metzudat David and Malbim identify these as the seats of the Sanhedrin and the judges of Israel; the second set, 'for the house of David', is the royal seat.

verses.translation_literal: Ask for the peace of Jerusalem: may they be at ease, those who love you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Ask for the peace of Jerusalem. Ask it, and let the asking be a blessing: may they rest easy, all who love you.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the turn of the psalm, from description to speech. Voice it as an instruction given to the whole company and then, in the second half, as words spoken straight to the city: 'those who love you', feminine singular, Jerusalem herself.

The sound carries the sense. Sha'alu, shalom, Yerushalayim, yishlayu: the sh and l keep returning, so that 'ask', 'peace', 'Jerusalem' and 'be at ease' all seem to be one word said four ways. English cannot keep that, so the actor must. The KJV's 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem' is a reasonable sense but a different verb; Hebrew says 'ask', and the commentators split on what asking means. Radak and Metzudat David take it as asking of God. 'Ask after her peace' may equally be the ordinary greeting, since asking after someone's shalom is how people greeted each other. Keep both in the air by playing 'ask' plainly and letting the audience decide. The second half is a wish, not a forecast: the KJV's 'they shall prosper that love thee' makes it a promise, and 'prosper' replaces a word about being at ease, calm and unthreatened, with one about wealth.

philological_notes.note: 'Ask for the peace of'. Metzudat David and Radak read the asking as asking of God, which is the KJV's 'pray'. The phrase may also be read as the everyday greeting idiom 'ask after the welfare of', which would make the line a salutation to the city as much as a prayer; this second reading is my own. The two words sound alike (sh-'-l, sh-l-m), and the sound play continues in Yerushalayim and yishlayu.

'May they be at ease': from shalah, to be quiet, secure, free of worry, not the root of 'peace' (shalom) though it sounds like it. Metzudat Zion ties it to shalvah, 'ease'. The KJV's 'prosper' reads it as material success.

verses.translation_literal: May there be peace in your rampart, ease in your fortresses.
verses.translation_dramatic: Peace on your ramparts. Ease in your strongholds, and quiet in every tower of you.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the blessing itself, spoken to the city, and its two halves go from the outside in: first the rampart, then the fortresses within. The ancient reader pictured a city in layers, with a low outer bank or glacis (חֵיל), the high wall behind it (חוֹמָה), and inside the walls the citadels. A blessing on the rampart is a blessing on the first thing an enemy would meet; a blessing on the citadels reaches the last place a siege would reach. It asks that peace should hold at every layer.

The KJV "within thy walls" and "palaces" mishear both words. חֵיל is not the main wall (that is חוֹמָה) but the outer rampart in front of it, as in Lam 2:8, which the commentators in the packet cite; and אַרְמוֹן is a fortified tower or citadel, a stronghold, though later Hebrew uses it for a palace, so KJV "palaces" and BBE's "noble houses" soften a military word into a luxurious one. The KJV also adds "prosperity" for שַׁלְוָה, which is "ease", not riches.

philological_notes.note: The outer rampart or glacis in front of the main wall, as in Lam 2:8 where it stands beside חוֹמָה. Not the same as 'army' (חַיִל), which is spelled almost alike. Radak and Metzudat Zion take it as the moat or the low outer wall.
'Citadels, fortified towers'; in later Hebrew also 'palace'. Metzudat Zion reads it as halls and palaces, Radak as fortified houses within the city.

verses.translation_literal: For the sake of my brothers and my friends, let me speak, please: peace in you.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the sake of my brothers, my friends, let me say it now: peace be in you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The pilgrim reveals who he is speaking for. He is not praying for himself but for the people he travels with, kin (אחים) and companions (רעים). Note the verb: "let me speak" is a cohortative with the polite particle "please" (נא), the tone of someone who steps forward and asks leave to say a thing that matters. Ancient travel to a festival was done in family and village groups, since the road was dangerous and company was safety, and the singer's "brothers" are the people on the road beside him.

The KJV "I will now say" turns "let me speak" into a flat statement and loses the deferential "please". The KJV also supplies "be" ("Peace be within thee"); the Hebrew has only "peace in you", a clipped greeting like a formula spoken at the door. Notice that the verb is דבר, "speak", not "say": a more formal and weighty word, one that Hebrew uses for a considered statement.

philological_notes.note: A cohortative ('let me speak') with the polite particle na ('please'). It is the voice of someone asking leave to speak. The KJV 'I will now say' drops the courtesy.
'My brothers and my friends': kin and companions. Rashi and Metzudat David read both as all Israel; Ibn Ezra as the priests, Levites and pious residents of Jerusalem.

verses.translation_literal: For the sake of the house of YHWH our God, I will seek good for you.
verses.translation_dramatic: And for the house of the LORD, our God, for its sake I will seek your good.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last line, and it should be the quietest. Verse 8 gave the first reason for the blessing, 'for the sake of my brothers and friends'; verse 9 gives the deeper one with the same opening word, lema'an, 'for the sake of'. The speaker's love of the city rests on the house of YHWH in it.

Listen for the frame. The psalm began with 'let us go to the house of YHWH' and 'our feet were standing'; it ends on 'the house of YHWH our God'. The 'we' of the opening returns in 'our God', and the pilgrim who set out in joy now stays to work for the city. The Hebrew 'I will seek' (avakshah) is a resolve, a cohortative, not the KJV's mild 'I will seek thy good': the speaker is volunteering. The KJV's 'the Lord' in small capitals hides that the name YHWH stands in the line, here made 'ours' by the possessive; keep the name as it is in the literal layer. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear the seeking as asking of God, Metzudat David ties it to the Temple that is to be built, and the actor may choose between them: they differ on what is sought, not on the motive.

philological_notes.note: 'For the sake of', opening both verse 8 and verse 9, so that the two verses are a matched pair: for the people, then for the house.

'I will seek': a first-person form with the ending -ah that expresses resolve, 'let me seek'. Radak reads the seeking as asking of the LORD for the city's good; Metzudat David attaches it to the house that is to be built there.
